extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and policymakers interested in political philosophy and freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical argument and set of practical principles defending unrestricted public discussion of opinions and the necessity of permitting challenge and criticism of received beliefs. The text illustrates why open debate is required to correct error, secure justified belief, and preserve intellectual vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrigibility as the basis of trust in human judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgment can be relied on only because errors are corrigible: people can rectify mistakes by discussion and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both discussion and experience are needed; facts rarely 'tell their own story' without commentary. To trust judgment, societies must keep available the means of setting judgments right. (Examples and explanation: the text argues that without the ability to correct errors by exposing them to criticism and interpreting experience via discussion, human opinion could not progressively improve.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain openness to criticism to attain wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: A person deserving of confidence keeps his mind open to criticism, listens to what can be said against him, profits by just criticisms, and exposes fallacies in what is fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wise thinkers collate their views with those of others and actively seek objections. The habit of soliciting and addressing counter-arguments provides a firmer basis for acting than unexamined certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow discussion on all doubtful matters; prohibition assumes infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rule forbidding the questioning of a doctrine because it is 'so certain' amounts to assuming infallibility on the part of those who enforce the prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anyone would deny a proposition when permitted but is not permitted, then to call the proposition certain is to assume that we (and our agreement) are the judges of certainty without hearing the other side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of an opinion is itself debatable and cannot justify silencing dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for suppressing opinions on the ground that they are useful to society are fallacious because the usefulness of an opinion is itself a matter of opinion requiring discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting debate on the basis of perceived social utility simply shifts the claim of infallibility to a different judgment; if utility is contested, it must be open to the same examination as truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit defenders of even sacred or moral doctrines to speak
rubrics_metrics.description: Even beliefs about God or fundamental morals must be allowed to be defended; preventing their defense for others is to decide those questions for them without hearing opposing reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists that forbidding dissent even about deeply held convictions (religion, morality) is especially dangerous—historical examples (Socrates, early Christians) show the tragic consequences of such suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: History shows persecution can suppress truth for long periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that truth always triumphs over persecution is false; persecution has repeatedly halted or delayed true opinions for centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited historical instances (e.g., repeated suppression of Reformation-like movements, the Albigeois, Lollards, Hussites, etc.) show persecution can succeed in extinguishing or delaying the public spread of true doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and social penalties that silence opinions are unjust and self-defeating
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and social rules that punish expression of opinion (for example, excluding unbelievers from juries or testimony) are discriminatory, irrational, and undermine justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives concrete legal examples (imprisonment in Cornwall for offensive words about Christianity; rejection of jurors for lack of theological belief; rule excluding non-believers' testimony) and argues such rules rest on absurd assumptions (e.g., that atheists must be liars) and harm both believers and non-believers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beliefs held without understanding grounds become dead dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: If an opinion is not frequently and fearlessly discussed, even if true it will be held as a dead dogma rather than a living truth; people ought to understand and be able to defend their beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely assenting to a doctrine without knowledge of its grounds is intellectually inferior—education and public debate should enable people to know and defend why they hold important beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must include exposure to opposing arguments (except where none exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching should include the reasons and objections for views so students understand the grounds of their opinions; unlike mathematics where all argument is one-sided, most subjects require balancing conflicting reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On subjects where difference of opinion is possible (morals, religion, politics, natural philosophy), learning only the affirmed side is insufficient; pupils must study adversary cases to grasp why rival explanations fail (Cicero's practice of studying his adversary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion is necessary to interpret experience and give facts meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts alone are often insufficient; discussion is needed to show how experience should be interpreted and to reveal the significance of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very few facts tell their own story without comments; public argument brings out meaning and allows facts and arguments to produce an effect on judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free debate cultivates intellectual courage and a lively public mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Silencing dissent produces conformity, timorous intellects, and time-servers; free and daring speculation is necessary to raise the general scale of mental activity in a people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When principles are tacitly undisputed, the populace lacks intellectual vigor. Periods of intellectual flourishing (post-Reformation, 18th-century speculation, German Goethian-Fichtean period) coincide with the breaking of authority's yoke and openness of debate.
